section_map.summary: The Summary moves from the VHF placement task and flat-terrain assumptions to a greedy population-aware coverage algorithm, graph coloring for frequencies, two synthetic population families, representative repeater counts, and a whole-region fallback bound.

The title and contents pages expose the full route from radio background and assumptions through circle covering, propagation, population generation, greedy coverage, utility, frequency coloring, experiments, terrain, conclusions, future work, and references.

The background explains the two-meter band, repeater input-output offsets, line-of-sight range, band plans, spatial frequency reuse, and EchoLink only far enough to derive range, spacing, channel, and connectivity assumptions.

The interpretation distinguishes 1,000 and 10,000 users, uniform and clustered populations, flat and mountainous regions, no-existing and partially-existing infrastructure, and the primary task of selecting sufficient repeaters and frequencies.

The assumptions fix an eighteen-foot antenna, a ten-mile ideal radius, a quarter-mile grid, circular propagation, independent failures, EchoLink interconnection, and a twenty-five-mile same-frequency separation rule before stating the model boundary.

The covering section first divides the area of a radius-forty disk by a radius-ten repeater disk to obtain a necessary lower bound of sixteen, then presents a hexagonal construction claimed to give an upper bound of twenty-one.

The propagation section explains inverse-square free-space loss, atmospheric refraction, radio horizon, two-ray ground reflection, diffraction, and Fresnel obstruction before returning to the circular approximation used in computation.

The population section contrasts uniform random users with a spatial clustering process that repeatedly chooses an existing user and places another nearby, then attempts to encode that process as pseudocode.

The main model states dual objectives—minimize repeaters for a required coverage fraction or maximize coverage for a fixed repeater count—then uses maximum marginal population coverage and derives a coarse fourth-order runtime.

The utility extension assigns diminishing value to redundant coverage under independent repeater downtime, identifies ordinary coverage as the zero-downtime special case, derives a target-utility iteration estimate, and supplies greedy pseudocode.

The noncircular extension replaces equal disks by arbitrary candidate coverage sets and states a complexity bound based on their largest-to-smallest area ratio before handing the selected repeaters to frequency assignment.
The frequency section constructs a conflict graph on selected repeaters, joins pairs within two-and-a-half radii, greedily colors the graph, and maps colors to frequencies.

The coverage results compare uniform and clustered populations at 1,000 and 10,000 users across increasing target ratios, reporting that the final approach to complete coverage causes a sharp rise in repeater count and that clustered users are easier to cover.

The utility results place coverage and utility curves in a common matrix, average repeated random runs, show one-standard-deviation error bars, and link selected repeater layouts to the number of graph colors.

The terrain section replaces circular reach by line-of-sight tests using bilinear interpolation or Bresenham sampling, derives a fifth-order all-pairs cost, defines a curved-earth surface, and perturbs it with Diamond-Square terrain.

The conclusion distinguishes the heuristic's value below complete coverage from a fixed whole-region fallback, reiterates the claimed frequency sufficiency, and summarizes flat-terrain findings before the future-work boundary.

Future work explicitly moves ad-hoc inter-repeater networking, one-to-one communication, dynamic users, correctness analysis, real topography, real population data, theory, and better algorithms outside the validated scope.

The references support network science, propagation, circle covering, hexagonal geometry, Longley-Rice, amateur-radio practice, and disk-covering algorithms but do not provide a reproducible data or code package.

assumptions.summary: An eighteen-foot antenna can be represented by a fixed ten-mile ideal coverage radius.
A quarter-mile grid adequately discretizes users and candidate repeater centers.
Coverage does not extend beyond the surrounding computational boundary.
One ideal repeater gives sufficient basic service to a covered user.
Repeater failures are independent and share one downtime parameter.
EchoLink makes users under different repeaters mutually reachable.
Buildings, local reflection, and diffraction can be ignored in the base flat model.
Two same-frequency repeaters must be separated by more than twenty-five miles.
Whole-region coverage can be bounded using equal ten-mile disks.
Synthetic uniform and clustered users stand in for real population data.
Choosing an existing user uniformly and placing another nearby creates a useful clustered population.
Maximum marginal coverage is an adequate heuristic for both coverage objectives.
Redundant coverage utility follows a geometric sequence under independent downtime.
Arbitrary noncircular coverage sets can be handled by the same marginal-gain framework.
A distance threshold of two-and-a-half radii defines relevant frequency conflicts.
Greedy graph colors can be mapped to usable frequencies.
Repeated synthetic runs reveal distribution and scale effects.
Terrain visibility can be reduced to sampled line-of-sight intersection tests.
A curved-earth surface plus Diamond-Square perturbations provides a useful synthetic terrain.
The fixed whole-region construction is a valid fallback when the population-aware greedy method is inefficient at complete coverage.

Selected repeater coordinates are converted into a geometric conflict graph.
Uniform and clustered populations at 1,000 and 10,000 users are repeatedly simulated.
Synthetic elevation combines a curved-earth base with Diamond-Square perturbations.

results_trace.summary: The Summary reports about fifteen repeaters for 1,000 users and twenty for 10,000 users without a fully specified result cell.
The Summary reports roughly ten and fifteen repeaters at 95 percent coverage for the two population sizes.
The covering section states a necessary lower bound of sixteen and a claimed feasible upper bound of twenty-one.
A 1,000-user uniform example uses 11, 15, and 28 repeaters at 80, 92, and 100 percent coverage.
A 10,000-user uniform example uses 12, 18, and 35 repeaters at 80, 92, and 100 percent coverage.
Clustered examples use fewer repeaters than comparable uniform examples and fewer graph colors.
Repeated-run curves rise with target ratio and shift upward when user count increases.
The final fraction of coverage causes the steepest increase in repeater count.
Utility examples report small color counts at selected target ratios.
The paper states that observed color counts rarely exceed twelve.
The greedy method can exceed the whole-region fallback at complete coverage.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A compact Summary that names assumptions, algorithm, frequency assignment, result scale, and fallback plausibly improves judge traceability, but its under-specified counts weaken confidence.
The dual-objective and special-case model structure is judge-friendly because it unifies basic and reliability-aware decisions, provided the pseudocode is corrected.
The matched result matrix and error bars plausibly strengthen comparison, but missing baselines and seeds prevent strong performance claims.

weaknesses.summary: The Summary says an eighteen-foot antenna produces a ten-mile range, while the displayed 1.41-sqrt(h) relation gives about 5.98 miles.
The representative counts near fifteen and twenty are not tied to a distribution, target ratio, utility parameter, or uncertainty.
The two horizon formulas use different constants without explaining effective-earth-radius or engineering conditions.
The dagger after Simplex has no matching dagger note on the page.
The claim that co-channel regions are about two hundred miles apart is not supported by the frequency-count table alone.
The eighteen-foot height and ten-mile radius are acknowledged as largely arbitrary rather than calibrated.
EchoLink externalizes inter-repeater wireless connectivity and changes the engineering problem.
The surrounding-grid boundary assumption may truncate coverage and bias edge candidates.
The twenty-five-mile same-frequency separation is not derived from the ten-mile radius or an interference model.
The area ratio supplies only a necessary lower bound and no construction for sixteen disks.
The description of the continuous disk-covering problem as simply unsolved and NP-complete needs a precise decision formulation and citation match.
Figure 3 appears to contain nineteen circles in a 3-4-5-4-3 arrangement while the text and caption claim twenty-one.
The hexagonal construction is an asserted feasible bound, not a proof that twenty-one is instance-optimal.
The inverse-fourth power relation is presented too generally; it is a two-ray far-field asymptote under specific conditions.
The uniform population generator is not specified; uniform radius sampling would bias points toward the center.
The spatial process is not classical Barabasi-Albert degree-proportional attachment despite using the name preferential attachment.
No displacement distribution, attachment radius, initial-user count, or random seed is reported.
Program 1 generates only initial users and then jumps to greedy graph coloring and frequency mapping.
Program 1 leaves total_users, r, and connect_chance unused and references undefined G and frequency_set.
The stated two-approximation requires a precise optimum k and applicability proof that the paper does not supply.
The basic O(s^4) derivation hides user count and candidate-evaluation data structures.
The probability that q independent repeaters all fail is p^q for one user, not n p^q; the latter can only resemble an expected count.
If layer utilities start at p, their geometric sum is p/(1-p), not 1/(1-p).
The downtime/utility parameter domain should be 0 <= u < 1 and the target ratio should satisfy 0 < W < 1.
Program 2 stops when current_utility/max_utility is below W, reversing the intended threshold logic.
Program 2 reuses u for downtime and candidate total utility, corrupting the subsequent user-utility update.
The optimized runtime claim lacks a precise update structure, memory cost, and proof.
The noncircular complexity ratio is undefined when min(a)=0 and is stated without derivation.
Greedy coloring does not define vertex order or a failure state when colors exceed available frequencies.
Program 3 colors a geometric conflict graph but does not map colors to legal duplex input/output pairs and guard bands.
Figure 8 is one illustrative realization, not a statistical or optimality validation.
Complete-coverage uniform examples require twenty-eight or thirty-five greedy repeaters, exceeding the separate whole-region bound and revealing heuristic inefficiency.
The experiments report standard deviations but no seeds, confidence intervals, convergence checks, or optimal baselines.
The 1,000-user cells use one hundred runs while the 10,000-user cells use twenty, complicating precision comparison.
Figures 13 and 14 label subplots as Coverage while their captions describe utility ratios.
The claim that twelve colors imply twelve feasible frequencies ignores channel spacing, protection, duplex pairing, and adjacent-channel interference.
The line-of-sight routine's expected constant-time claim lacks a terrain distribution or early-termination argument.
The O(n^5) claim depends on interpreting n as the side length of an n by n grid; the paper's size definition is ambiguous.
The printed terrain-surface offset and sign are not reconciled with the stated distance-from-earth-center axis.
Figure 15 demonstrates terrain generation but provides no mountainous coverage or repeater-count experiment.
The conclusion calls the Section 4 construction optimal even though only a claimed upper bound was presented.
The statement that twenty-one repeaters always suffice is limited to equal ten-mile disks on the flat idealized domain, not terrain line of sight.
The claim of knowing an optimal solution for most population distributions is not supported by the greedy experiments.
The references provide background but no executable code, generated datasets, seeds, or complete reproducibility package.

independent_extensions.summary: Calibrate coverage with a bidirectional VHF link budget, effective-earth-radius horizon, antenna patterns, clutter, fading margin, and measured drive-test data.
Verify the whole-region construction computationally from explicit circle centers and separate feasibility, lower bounds, and instance optimality.
Specify uniform and clustered population generators with correct area sampling, displacement distributions, seeds, and spatial summary diagnostics.
Repair and implement the coverage and utility algorithms with typed variables, tested stop rules, incremental gain updates, and small-instance optimum comparisons.
Construct a legal duplex frequency plan with channel bandwidth, guard bands, spatial reuse, adjacent-channel constraints, and coloring failure handling.
Run seed-controlled experiments with confidence intervals, optimum or approximation baselines, sensitivity to grid spacing, and fairness or worst-served-user metrics.
Use measured DEM and population data with Longley-Rice or calibrated line-of-sight propagation, spatial indexing, and quantitative terrain placement comparisons.
